entry.title: Handing my mail to coding agents, and keeping Send for myself
entry.summary: Yardlet 0.11.8 adds a mailbox for Gmail, Outlook and IMAP accounts. Agents read a thread and write the reply as a draft through the account's connector; every send goes through the agent's approval.
entry.content:
I make Yardlet, a free, open-source Mac app that runs coding agents like Codex and Claude Code in one window.

I used to do my mail in Apple Mail. When I moved to a new Mac this week, my accounts didn't come over with it, and while setting them up again I realized I hadn't been reading mail there or writing replies there for a while. Agents in Yardlet were reading the threads through its Gmail and Outlook connectors and writing the replies as drafts. The mail app wasn't where I worked with mail anymore, so mail belonged in the workbench, next to the agents.

Yardlet 0.11.8 adds a mailbox. It is off by default. Settings › General › Mailbox turns it on, and the sidebar gets Mail next to Tasks and Personal agents. This post covers what it keeps, how a thread gets to an agent, who presses Send, and why Naver Mail needed IMAP.

#It reads the service and keeps almost nothing

The mailbox uses the sign-in the connector already has. Gmail is read through the Gmail API with the gmail.modify scope the connector asked for, Outlook through Microsoft Graph with Mail.ReadWrite and Mail.Send. Nothing more is requested, and the connector and the mailbox share one token.

Mail stays on the service. The mailbox reads a list when it is shown and keeps it in memory: the first page of each inbox, the folders a window opened, the last 30 threads. On disk it writes one thing per account, how far it has read the inbox's history (a Gmail history ID, a Graph delta link, an IMAP inbox's next UID), so mail that came while Yardlet was closed is still announced. No subject, address or line of a message goes to disk or to the log.

New mail is checked once a minute: users.history.list for Gmail, which costs 2 quota units, the inbox's delta query for Outlook, STATUS for IMAP. No model is involved. Mail that lands in Gmail's Primary tab or Outlook's Focused inbox becomes a notification.

HTML mail is drawn with scripts off, no cookies or storage, and a content rule that blocks every http and https load until I choose Show images for that message, so a tracking pixel has nothing to report. If the rule can't be compiled, the message is shown as text.

#Handing a thread to an agent

Ask an agent on a thread opens a new chat with the thread named in the composer:

Then I write what I want done. The message itself is not pasted in. The agent reads it with the connector tool on that line, so it sees the thread as the account has it now, and a stranger's words don't land where my instructions go.

From there the agent works with the connector's tools as before. It can search the account, read other threads for context, and write a reply with create_draft. The draft is saved in the account's own Drafts folder, so it shows in the thread in the mailbox, under an orange Draft, and in any other app that reads the account.

#Who presses Send

On a draft in the mailbox I get Send, Edit and Discard. Send sends the draft as it was saved, so an HTML reply the agent wrote goes out as it is. Edit continues it as plain text with its recipients, blind copies and files. My own Send waits five seconds, during which Undo brings the message back.

The agent can send too, but not on its own say. The send tools (send_draft and send_message) are on the list of tools that go through the agent's approval each time. In Claude Code the request card has no "Always allow". For Gmail and Outlook it shows the recipients, the subject and the first 1,200 characters of the body, and when the agent sends a Gmail draft by its ID, Yardlet reads the draft from Gmail first and shows it instead of the ID. Codex decides from the task's approval settings and the tools' annotations, and ACP agents use their own MCP approval. Yardlet keeps no approval rules of its own. A task running with permissions bypassed is not asked, for these tools as for any other.

#Naver Mail has no API

Gmail and Outlook have APIs. A lot of mail in Korea lives at Naver, Daum or Kakao, and none of them has an API that Yardlet can read mail through. What they all have is IMAP and SMTP with an app password, the way Apple Mail and Thunderbird add them. So that is the third kind of account: Settings › Connectors › Add connector › Mail (IMAP).

I type the address, and the address picks the service: its IMAP and SMTP servers, the user name (for iCloud, the part before the @), and what the service wants done on its website first, each step with a link. Usually that is turning on two-step verification, making an app password, and for Naver, Daum, Kakao and Zoho, switching IMAP on. NAVER WORKS, iCloud, Yahoo, AOL, Fastmail and Proton Mail Bridge are on the list too, and Other IMAP server takes the servers by hand.

Connect signs in to the IMAP server and to the SMTP server once each and signs out again, reading and sending nothing. Only when both accept the password is the account added. The app password goes into the Keychain and nowhere else, not into a file, the log or a command line. The servers and the address aren't secret, so they're in the connector's record. Every connection is TLS from the first byte or upgraded with STARTTLS before signing in, with the certificate checked against the server's name; a server that offers neither isn't used.

IMAP leaves more to the client than the APIs do. It has no threads, so each message is a line of its own. Folders are found by their special-use flags, or by the names services give them in English and Korean (보낸편지함, 임시보관함, 스팸편지함, 휴지통), and their names come in IMAP's modified UTF-7. Messages are read with BODY.PEEK, so opening one doesn't mark it read unless I opened it in the mailbox. A draft is a message appended to Drafts with its own From, Date and Message-ID. Sending goes over SMTP to every recipient with the Bcc line taken out, and a copy goes into Sent unless the server already put one there, found by its Message-ID.

Agents get five tools for such an account, named like Outlook's: search_messages, get_message, list_folders, create_draft and send_draft. There is no delete, and send_draft asks before every call.

#Turning it off

Turning the mailbox off stops the check, closes what's open, forgets every list and thread and the message being written, and removes the history markers on disk. The connectors and their Keychain items stay, since they belong to Settings › Connectors, where removing an IMAP account deletes its password too. The app password itself stays valid at the service until you delete it there.

The mailbox is documented in docs/MAILBOX.md, and the connector side in docs/CONNECTORS.md.

entry.title: Giving coding agents an MCP server without writing to their settings
entry.summary: Yardlet hands Codex, Claude Code and ACP agents its MCP server one session at a time: a launch argument for one, a request field for the others. Nothing is written to their settings.
entry.content:
I make Yardlet, a free, open-source Mac app that runs coding agents like Codex and Claude Code in one window. The agents get a few tools from it: a browser panel they can drive while I watch, a view of my other tasks, and the connectors I signed in to once. All of that comes through one small MCP server in the app bundle, yardlet-mcp.

The usual way to give an agent an MCP server is to register it in the agent's settings: claude mcp add for Claude Code, an mcp_servers entry in config.toml for Codex. Yardlet doesn't. It passes the server to each session as it starts, through whatever that agent accepts for one session. This post is about why, and what each agent accepts.

#Why not the settings file

Early on I considered things that would have made Yardlet matter more to the agent: a hook that handles approvals, performance numbers sent with every turn. I dropped them. Yardlet runs each agent's own CLI, and what it changes for a session, it changes in that process only, with an argument or an environment variable. I wanted two things to hold:

  • What Yardlet adds, you can switch off in its settings, and the agent's own files don't change either way.
  • Quit Yardlet or drag it to the Trash, and the agents, their sign-ins and their sessions are as they were.

A server in the agent's settings would break the second one. Every session, in Yardlet or not, would start the server. With Yardlet closed, it would still list its browser tools and answer every call with an error. Remove the app, and the entry stays, pointing at a command that is gone.

#What each agent accepts for one session

Claude Code takes --mcp-config <file>. Yardlet writes one file per session, with the server and the session's token in its environment:

A JSON argument would work too, but then the token would show in the process list. So the file sits in a folder only the user can open, under the temporary directory of that run of Yardlet. It goes when Yardlet quits; a run that crashed leaves it, and the next run removes it. The argument goes last, because it takes several values, so nothing after it is taken as one of them. I don't pass --strict-mcp-config, which would drop the servers you registered yourself. They load beside Yardlet's, with one exception: when a Yardlet connector is connected for the same address as one of your Claude servers, that server is denied for this process through --settings, so the agent isn't offered the same service twice. That is a launch argument too.

Codex runs as an App Server, and thread/start, thread/resume and thread/fork take a config object for that thread:

Codex merges it over the user's configuration. I checked with a server of my own in the config.toml of a temporary home: mcpServerStatus/list showed both connected. The timeout is there because a browser call can wait for a page to load, longer than Codex's default.

ACP agents (OpenCode, Kimi Code, Grok Build, Hermes) take mcpServers in session/new and session/load. The protocol makes stdio servers mandatory for them. OpenCode, in a temporary home, started the server from that field and asked it for the tool list.

Cursor Agent, Antigravity CLI, Pi and Muse Code don't have one. The interfaces Yardlet runs them through have no field for a session's MCP servers; what they load comes from their configuration. Their tasks in Yardlet run without the tools. I'd rather leave those tasks without the tools than write to the agents' settings.

#Antigravity loaded it, and kept a note

Antigravity nearly worked. Its CLI loads .agents/mcp_config.json from any folder passed with --add-dir, so Yardlet could pass a folder of its own, and the server loaded. Then I looked at what the CLI writes down. It records the folder in the conversation's workspace_uris, and when you continue that conversation in a terminal, it brings the folder back and tries to load the server again. A conversation continued outside Yardlet still made the CLI try to load Yardlet's server. I reverted that the same day, before it reached a release.

Since then the question I ask is not whether the server loads but what the agent writes down about it. For the three above, the server is in none of their files. Their transcripts keep the calls the agent made to the tools, as they keep any tool call; a session resumed outside Yardlet simply doesn't have the tools any more.

#Keeping the token to its session

The server itself does little. It asks the running app for the task's tool list and forwards each call over a local socket; the app drives the browser and the connectors. Each session gets a random 256-bit token in the server's environment. The app runs a call only when the token and the task ID match and the process that connected runs under the agent Yardlet runs for it: that task's Claude Code process, one of the Codex App Servers Yardlet started, or Yardlet itself for an ACP agent. Another process of the same user could read the token from the environment, but not call with it from elsewhere. Approvals stay with the agent, Claude's permission card or Codex's approval policy; Yardlet doesn't ask a second time.

#What is left when you remove it

Nothing in the agents' settings. Yardlet's own things are listed in the README: ~/.yardlet (tasks, drafts), ~/Library/Application Support/Yardlet (browser profiles), its logs and caches, and the Keychain items named Yardlet for the connectors. If you enabled the option to keep tasks running with the lid closed, turn it off before deleting the app. macOS keeps the app's background item after the app is gone.

entry.title: A Logger symbol missing on macOS 15 kept my Mac app from launching
entry.summary: For four days Yardlet quit at launch on macOS 15. The SDK marks Logger.isEnabled(type:) as available since macOS 11, but macOS 15.6.1's libswiftos doesn't have it.
entry.content:
I make Yardlet, a free, open-source Mac app for running coding agents like Codex and Claude Code in one window. It says it needs macOS 15 or later. For four days it quit at launch on macOS 15, and I didn't know.

#How I found out

On October 31 I was getting my company MacBook ready for a performance comparison. That Mac is still on macOS 15.6.1. Yardlet quit the moment it launched. No window, just a crash report. My first thought was that the company Mac was just too old.

That symbol is Logger.isEnabled(type:) from the os module. I used it in one place, to skip building debug messages about text selection when nobody is reading debug logs.

I downloaded the public disk images of 0.11.0, 0.11.4 and 0.11.5 and checked them with nm -u. All three import it. 0.11.0, the first public release, went out on October 27. My own Mac runs macOS 27, so I never saw it.

#Why it compiled

The deployment target is macOS 15, so I expected an availability error if I called anything newer. In Xcode 27.1's SDK, Logger is marked available since macOS 11, and isEnabled(type:) has no availability of its own (shortened):

So the compiler treats it as there since macOS 11. But the macOS 15.5 SDK that comes with the Command Line Tools has no such symbol in libswiftos.tbd, the 27 SDK has it, and libswiftos.dylib on macOS 15.6.1 doesn't export it. I haven't checked macOS 26.

#The fix

OSLog has its own isEnabled(type:), which goes to the C function os_log_type_enabled, there since macOS 10.12. So I keep an OSLog handle, make the Logger from it, and ask the handle:

#Checking the other imports

I didn't want to find the next one the same way. On the macOS 15.6.1 Mac I listed the symbols the executable imports without weak linking, and checked each one against what its system library exports there. A rough version of the script (it doesn't check exit codes):

It follows direct re-exports, since SwiftUI re-exports SwiftUICore on macOS 15. For 0.11.5, with 4,261 strong imports, it printed one line: libswiftos os.Logger.isEnabled(type: __C.os_log_type_t) -> Swift.Bool.

0.11.6 went out the same night. Before publishing it I copied the notarized disk image to the macOS 15.6.1 Mac. The script printed nothing for its 4,291 imports, and the app stayed up when I launched it with an empty home folder.

#What changed

Now every release gets this check and a launch on that macOS 15 Mac before it goes out. A CI job that launches the app on the oldest supported macOS is planned but not built yet.

I had thought of the deployment target as something the compiler would hold me to. It only holds me to what the SDK says, and here that was macOS 11.
